definition: A computing system of connected units (“neurons”) organized in layers that learns by adjusting connection weights.
details: Inspired by biological neurons, the perceptron showed a single weighted unit could learn simple classifications. Stacking such units into layers — with nonlinear activations — lets networks approximate complex functions, and modern neural networks learn their own internal features from raw data.

explainer.lead: A neural network is a computing system of connected units in layers that learns by adjusting connection weights. It matters because layering nonlinear units lets it approximate complex functions and learn its own features from raw data.

tiers.eli5: It's layers of little units that pass signals along, and learning means nudging how strongly each one listens until the answers come out right.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers stack layers with nonlinear activations and train the weights on data, letting the network learn internal features rather than hand-crafting them. A pitfall is that a single unit only handles simple classifications, so depth and nonlinearity are needed for complex tasks.
tiers.paperLevel: A network is a system of connected units organised in layers; the perceptron showed a single weighted unit could learn simple classifications, and stacking units with nonlinear activations lets networks approximate complex functions.

explainer.example: A single perceptron can separate two simple classes, but stacking such units into layers with nonlinear activations lets the network approximate a far more complex decision boundary from raw data.

citation.title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain
